newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-INSTANT VIEW-Australian December quarter GDP.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-INSTANT VIEW-Australian December quarter GDP.

text.p: The average measure of Australian gross domestic product (GDP) rose 0.5 percent in the December quarter to be 3.1 percent higher over the previous 12 months, the Australian Bureau of Statistics reported.
September quarter growth was revised down to 0.6 percent from an originally published 0.8 percent.
Income-based GDP rose 0.8 percent in the quarter, expenditure based GDP was flat and the production based measure was up 0.6 percent.
The GDP-E deflator rose 0.4 percent in the quarter.
A selection of economists reactions to the data follows.
CHRIS CATON, CHIEF ECONOMIST, BANKERS TRUST AUSTRALIA:

"Well, I think it really confirms what we already knew, that we ended 1996 with the economy in quite a soft state. For the past three quarters, beginning in June quarter of last year, we saw 0.3, 06 and then 0.5 (percent growth) in GDP(A), and that's clearly a soft picture. And incidentally, this number makes it pretty hard to get to the government's forecast of 3.5 (percent growth for all of 96/97."
ROBIN LARSEN, SENIOR ECONOMIST, ANZ BANKING GROUP:

"It was pretty close to the market consensus, a little bit stronger than we had factored in. Even the revision of the September quarter was not surprsing. The market hasn't reacted very much to it and I don't expect it should. It just confirms that the economy slowed substantially in the second half of 1996 from the second half and that was probably the low point of the cycle."
BRUCE FREELAND, CHIEF ECONOMIST, COMMONWEALTH BANK:

"The breakdown, and particularly the weakness in the expenditure based measure of GDP, that really I think reflects the quite soft state of the domestic economy in the December quarter. The income measure (was) stronger as expected, really reflecting the stronger profit performance and a bit of a pick up in wages and employment that we've been seeing in that last quarter of the year. They are largely historical, and they were telling us what the other partial indicators had already told us, that the economy was soft in December. Yesterday's retail trade are more telling about the pick up that I think is now underway, but they (the GDP data) also were telling us that inflation was quite g
NIGEL STAPLEDON, CHIEF ECONOMIST, WESTPAC BANKING CORP:

"GDP-A for the quarter is in line with expectations, but bearing in mind the downwards revisions to the past quarters, which are just a bit below expectations, so the 3.1 percent annual change is below expectations which were at 3.5 percent. It's basically a good result because you have some very good numbers on the deflators and pretty modest growth. The only real surprise is that consumption spending managed to grow 0.5 percent despite the sharp fall in retail spending. This is a fairly neutral result for the market. It's not going to move one way or the other on the back of this number."
ANNETTE BEACHER, SENIOR ECONOMIST, CITIBANK AUSTRALIA:

"All the pieces we have seen over the last four weeks or so have come to fruition. There are no surprises at all. The only real good news is on the deflator side, but even that's not new. There's obviously a revision to history somewhere along the line because 0.5 percent was supposed to equal to 3.5 percent year-on-year. Given the figures for January we have seen so far, I think we can expect a reversal of that weak private consumption."
RIC SIMES, CHIEF ECONOMIST, ROTHSCHILD AUSTRALIA:

"GDP(A), both in the December quarter and revisions to the previous few quarters, bring the picture for GDP back down to a level that's more consistent with the anecdotal evidence that you were getting. What you have is the year-to number is now 3.1 percent, with three very subdued quarters -- June, September and December -- and that's broadly consistent with what was going on in the labour market, and broadly consistent with the general tone of the economy through that period. That is modest growth through it, but only modest growth. The deflators fit in with the notion that inflation is under control for a while."
JOHN KYRIAKOPOULOS, SENIOR ECONOMIST, MACQUARIE BANK:

"It was in line with the market expectation, but if you look below the surface, consumption, the area people thought should have been weak, was a bit better. Housing had a small contribution, and we know that since then January building approvals data has risen sharply, and we are just going to get continual positive contributions from housing to the economy."
HANS KUNNEN, CHIEF ECONOMIST, COLONIAL STATE BANK:

"The most exciting thing for us was the deflator figures, point-two for consumption and point-four for overall, which really confirms and rams home to the masses that inflation is low and we think it is likely to stay that way. The revision to previous quarters GDP are confusing for everybody but this would appear to be at the bottom of the cycle at 3.1 (percent annual gdp growth). It is below par but not bad, we think that interest rate (cuts) that have occurred will push that figure up over the next few quarters. Australia is capable of doing far better than 3.1 (GDP annual growth). The bond dealers are more worried about (U.S. Fed governor) Greenspan and U.S. job growth figures than r
IVAN COLHOUN, ASSOCIATE DIRECTOR, DEUTSCHE MORGAN GRENFELL"

"It was the December quarter and the year to December quarter was pretty weak and in that regard it has come in at point-five. So it wasn't a disastrous quarter, it was probably a little bit stronger. The things that we liked in it in terms of the growth view was that private consumption was stronger than retail sales, considerably stronger. All of these components of private consumption, mainly services, that weren't retail sales are doing a lot better than retail sales. And that could be an issue for retailers, i.e. people are paying more money on gambling and entertainment -- lots of different things."
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
